1.referenceTitle: FDA Human Foods Program 2026 priority deliverables
1.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Human Foods Program 2026 Priority Deliverables. 2026 program work plan; accessed September 15, 2026.
1.summary: FDA identifies work toward cadmium and inorganic-arsenic action levels for baby and toddler foods, alongside chemical-hazard guidance, surveillance and infant-formula initiatives.
1.establishes: The page establishes planned agency work. It does not itself adopt numeric limits, establish a completion date or determine the legal effect of a future instrument.
1.relevance: This supports the article’s separation of policy plans from operative state duties. HMTc should review an issued instrument before treating a planned action level as a standard input.

evidence.note: Read introduction, Food Chemical Safety/Closer to Zero and Infant Formula Safety priorities. 2.referenceTitle: Virginia Code section 3.2-5125.1, Baby Food Protection Act
2.citation: Virginia Code §3.2-5125.1, Baby Food Protection Act; 2025 Virginia Acts chapter 693 (HB1844), approved May 2, 2025; substantive provisions effective January 1, 2026.
2.summary: The law covers specified packaged foods sold for children under two and excludes infant formula. It requires representative production-aggregate testing at least monthly, qualified laboratories, public results for shelf life plus one month, and conditional package QR disclosures.
2.establishes: It also restricts sales above FDA-established limits, preserving certain retailer inventory from before January 2026. The text supplies state duties, not a new numerical table for every metal or automatic certification compliance.
2.relevance: HMTc evidence must map the product definition, four listed metals, sample identity, laboratory requirements and disclosure trigger. A passing certification result alone does not discharge these operational duties.

evidence.note: Read complete subsectionsA–F: arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury; ISO 17025:2017 accreditation plus method sensitivity and proficiency requirements; public website and conditional QR provisions. No assertion made that every FDA guidance number necessarily qualifies as a sale limit.

Read both pages of official chapter 693, matched title/HB1844 and approvalMay2, 2025. Enactment2 specifies January 1, 2026 for first-enactment provisions; §B preserves retailer inventory already in stock before that date. Separate work-group clause is not a product limit.

3.referenceTitle: Illinois SB0073 bill status and Public Act record
3.citation: Illinois Public Act 104-0345 (SB0073), codified at 410 ILCS 620/11.7, Baby foods; toxic elements. Effective January 1, 2026; consumer disclosure begins January 1, 2027.
3.summary: The enacted section requires representative testing of every production aggregate at least monthly by a proficient laboratory. It covers packaged foods for children under two, excludes formula, and sets later website and conditional QR-label disclosure duties.
3.establishes: The sale restriction enforces compliance with this section; the final text does not reproduce the introduced bill’s blanket FDA-limit sale prohibition. January 2026 effectiveness must be separated from January 2027 disclosure.
3.relevance: This supports the article’s state-specific evidence matrix. HMTc should preserve lot results and laboratory qualifications while scheduling the Illinois disclosure requirement separately.

5.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA’s Infant Formula Product Testing Results. 2026 release reporting the FY2023–2025 market-basket survey; accessed September 15, 2026.
5.summary: FDA reports 312 samples across 16 brands, including powder and liquid formula. The page summarizes metals and other contaminants, expresses metal results as prepared for feeding, and describes follow-up testing.
5.establishes: This is occurrence monitoring, not a new legal limit. FDA cautions that a retail snapshot cannot capture all variability among production lots and that detection alone does not establish an unsafe product.
5.relevance: The source supports the article’s evidence-versus-law distinction. HMTc can use it for surveillance context while retaining separate lot-specific testing and jurisdictional requirements.
